# Abstract

This study compares four collaborative filtering approaches for book recommendation systems using a modified Book-Crossing dataset (45,370 ratings, 10,000 users, 145 books). We implement item-based (IBCF) and user-based (UBCF) collaborative filtering from scratch, alongside matrix factorization (MF) and neural network (NN) models. Results show matrix factorization achieves the lowest prediction error (RMSE = 1.820), while incorporating confidence-weighted similarity improves memory-based methods by leveraging implicit feedback. Accuracy gains plateau around 50 titles, suggesting diminishing returns beyond this range. These findings offer practical guidance for designing efficient hybrid recommenders in high-sparsity environments.

# 1. Introduction

Recommender systems help users navigate information overload by predicting preferences based on patterns in user–item interactions. Collaborative filtering (CF), a widely used approach, infers user interests from historical behavior and powers major platforms such as Amazon and Netflix, enhancing engagement through personalized suggestions.

This study employs a modified Book-Crossing dataset containing 45,370 ratings from 10,000 users across 145 books. Ratings range from 0 to 10, with 0 representing implicit feedback ("read but not rated") and 1–10 representing explicit evaluations. The combination of explicit and implicit ratings presents challenges for collaborative filtering in sparse environments, requiring strategies to extract meaningful signals from limited data.

The objectives of this study are to: (1) implement and evaluate four collaborative filtering methods—user-based (UBCF), item-based (IBCF), matrix factorization (MF), and neural network-based (NN); (2) compare their predictive performance using cross-validation; (3) assess robustness to cold-start scenarios; and (4) investigate how catalog size affects prediction accuracy.

Memory-based methods (UBCF and IBCF) rely on similarity computations directly from the user–item matrix, while model-based approaches (MF and NN) learn latent representations that capture hidden preference patterns in lower-dimensional spaces. To address sparsity and incorporate implicit feedback, we employ confidence-weighted similarity measures, enabling more accurate and robust recommendations across diverse scenarios.

# 2. Data Understanding and Preparation

## 2.1 Data Description

The dataset consists of three components: book_ratings, which records user–book interactions with variables User.ID, ISBN, and Book.Rating on a 0–10 scale; book_info, which provides metadata such as Book.Title and Book.Author; and user_info, which contains limited demographic details like age but is excluded from this analysis to focus on collaborative filtering. Ratings from 1–10 represent explicit feedback, where users actively rated books, while a rating of 0 indicates implicit feedback, meaning the user read the book but did not provide a score.

## 2.2 Exploratory Data Analysis

As shown in Table 1, the dataset contains 10,000 users, 145 books, and 45,370 interactions, with an average rating of 3.16 (including implicit ratings) and 7.8 for explicit ratings. Matrix sparsity is high (96.87% before filtering, 99.2% after), posing challenges for collaborative filtering and motivating our confidence-weighting approach. 

The dataset exhibits typical recommendation system characteristics (Figure 1): Panel A shows a right-skewed distribution of explicit ratings (mean 7.8), reflecting a positivity bias; Panel B shows a long-tail user activity distribution, with most users rating <10 books; Panel C indicates no strong correlation between book popularity and average rating, reducing popularity bias; Panel D reveals 40.3% explicit and 59.7% implicit ratings. Confidence weighting (1.0 for explicit, 0.5 for implicit, with implicit ratings converted to 4) allows leveraging all feedback while appropriately down-weighting less informative signals.

## 2.3 Data Preprocessing and Filtering

Duplicate book entries, where the same title and author appeared under different ISBNs, were identified using normalized string matching and consolidated to a canonical ISBN, with each user's highest rating retained.

To ensure reliable collaborative filtering, books with ≥5 ratings and users with ≥3 ratings were retained, resulting in 4,200 active users (58% of users excluded) and all 145 books included.

# 3. Methodology

## 3.1 Evaluation Framework

Performance was evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation with RMSE as the primary metric, calculated only on explicit ratings (1–10) to assess true prediction accuracy. In each fold, 80% of ratings were used for training and 20% for testing, with test values temporarily set to NA to prevent leakage. Confidence weighting was applied consistently to memory-based methods for fair comparison.

## 3.2 User-Item Matrix Construction and Implicit Feedback

Three matrices managed mixed feedback. Implicit ratings were converted to 4 in the ratings matrix, a confidence matrix weighted explicit ratings 1.0 and implicit 0.5 for similarity calculations, and the original matrix retained raw values for RMSE evaluation, enabling sparsity handling while leveraging all interactions.

## 3.3 Collaborative Filtering Approaches

### 3.3.1 User-Based Collaborative Filtering (UBCF)

UBCF estimates ratings by leveraging similar users' preferences. User-mean normalization removed individual biases, confidence-weighted cosine similarity identified similar users, and k=50 nearest neighbors generated predictions combining target user's mean with weighted averages from similar users.

### 3.3.2 Item-Based Collaborative Filtering (IBCF)

IBCF uses item similarity rather than user similarity. Item-mean normalization removed popularity biases, confidence-weighted cosine similarity computed item relationships, and k=50 neighbors aggregated the target user's ratings for similar items.

### 3.3.3 Matrix Factorization (MF)

MF decomposes the rating matrix into lower-dimensional latent factors using recosystem with parallel stochastic gradient descent. Grid search optimized latent dimensions (10, 20, 30), learning rates (0.01-0.1), and L2 regularization (0.01-0.1). Models trained for 100 iterations using 4 threads on explicit ratings only.

### 3.3.4 Neural Network-Based Collaborative Filtering (NN)

NN-based CF used H2O's deep learning framework with user-mean normalization. Grid search evaluated 24 configurations across layer depths (1-3), hidden units (16-128), activation functions (Tanh, ReLU), and regularization strengths (0.00001-0.0001).

## 3.4 Cold Start Evaluation

We created a synthetic new user with 5 book ratings [7, 8, 6, 5, 7]. Memory-based methods computed similarities on-the-fly from available ratings. MF used hybrid approach with user bias (difference between user mean and global mean). NN applied similarity-based fallback using top 30 similar users.

## 3.5 Catalog Size Impact Analysis

We varied catalog size (N ∈ {5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120, 130, 145}) using most popular books. Users required ≥3 ratings per catalog. Analysis repeated across 5 random seeds with mean RMSE and standard error computed.

# 4. Results and Evaluation

## 4.1 Cross-Validation Performance

Matrix Factorization achieved lowest RMSE of 1.820 (SD = 0.020), followed by Neural Networks at 1.899 (SD = 0.053). Item-Based CF achieved 2.746 (SD = 0.018), while User-Based CF recorded 3.182 (SD = 0.047). The 43% reduction in error between best and worst methods highlights algorithm importance in sparse datasets.

## 4.2 Cold Start Analysis

Analyzing 40 total recommendations (10 per method) revealed only 17.5% overlap, indicating substantial algorithmic divergence. Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix appeared in three methods (UBCF: 7.34, IBCF: 7.03, NN: 6.50), representing highest consensus. Six titles appeared in exactly two methods with notably different predicted ratings, suggesting different confidence calibrations.

## 4.3 Catalog Size Impact

MF achieved optimal performance at 50 books (RMSE = 1.815 ± 0.027), representing 10.4% improvement over 5 books (RMSE = 2.027). Performance remained stable across 40-60 books. Sharp improvement occurred between 5-10 books (7.3% reduction). At full catalog (145 books), RMSE rose slightly to 1.833, indicating diminishing returns beyond 50-60 items. Optimal performance at 86.7% sparsity demonstrates MF's effectiveness in sparse environments.

# 5. Discussion

## 5.1 Comparative Performance

Model-based methods substantially outperformed memory-based ones, confirming superior robustness to sparsity. MF achieved best accuracy-stability balance. The 43% performance gap underscores how algorithmic structure shapes accuracy under sparse conditions. IBCF outperformed UBCF as item relationships prove more stable than user relationships.

## 5.2 Catalog Size Dynamics

Non-monotonic relationship revealed optimal performance at 50 books before plateauing. Improvement phase (5→50 books) enabled better latent factor estimation. Beyond this threshold, less-rated titles introduced noise. Decreasing variability beyond 50 books (SE < 0.03) reflects greater stability with sufficient data density.

## 5.3 Recommendation Divergence

82.5% uniqueness highlights fundamental differences in preference modeling. Memory-based methods operate on orthogonal principles (user similarity vs. item co-occurrence), explaining minimal overlap. Model-based approaches infer latent structures differently—MF captures linear relationships while NN reveals nonlinear interactions. Rating discrepancies for shared titles (up to 1.36 points) suggest distinct confidence calibrations.

## 5.4 Cold-Start Limitations

Model-based methods required simplified fallback strategies differing from core mechanisms, limiting interpretability. This reveals a fundamental trade-off: model-based methods achieve superior accuracy for existing users but need auxiliary strategies for new ones, while memory-based methods remain algorithmically consistent. Practical systems require hybrid solutions integrating content-based features or transfer learning.

# 6. Conclusion

This study implemented and evaluated four collaborative filtering approaches for book recommendations, providing key insights for system design. Matrix Factorization was the most accurate method (RMSE = 1.820), while confidence-weighted similarity effectively leveraged implicit feedback to enhance memory-based methods. Catalog size analysis showed that accuracy gains plateaued beyond 50–60 books, indicating that near-optimal performance can be achieved without expansive catalogs.

Limitations include the 145-book dataset, which may not capture full recommendation diversity, the need for refined handling of implicit feedback, and suboptimal cold-start strategies for model-based systems that do not fully exploit learned representations. Future work should explore hybrid ensembles combining complementary methods, advanced deep learning architectures (autoencoders, attention mechanisms), context-aware metadata (genres, authors, temporal patterns), and online learning for real-time adaptation. Overall, this study offers both theoretical insights and practical guidance for developing production-ready recommendation systems across domains.
